candidates.author: Eva Ayub
candidates.description:
All images here are of Karura Forest in Nairobi, Kenya. The photos portray a vast forest area comprising of a variety of Plant species- mainly trees like Olea europaea (var. africana), Croton megalocarpus and many more and a lot of grasses and thickets.
The photos also portray the beautiful waterfall within the forest and the nature trail where civilians are allowed to walk through as you'll note- some individuals captured in the photos. 
Some of the photos capture the rules put in place by the Forest Management like one to avoid entry towards the Waterfall- which usually gets crowded in a bid to curb the ongoing spread of the highly infectious Corona Virus disease.
The photo gallery size in totality is about 209MBs but each individual photo is just about 4MBs for the smaller sized ones and about 9MBs for the larger sized ones. The photo format for the images is JPG. All images shared here are captured on an iPhone 8 with a 12-megapixel rear-facing camera.
Geographical coordinates for Karura Forest are:
DMS   1° 14′ 25″ S, 36° 49′ 25″ E
Decimal  -1.240278, 36.823611	

Geo URI	geo:-1.240278,36.823611

UTM    37M 257820 9862812

Date photos were taken: 30th July 2019

candidates.fileTitle: File:Misspelt Princes (Princess) Street sign in Frederick Street, Edinburgh, 26 December 2009.jpg
candidates.author: Зеленый кабинет
candidates.description: The view south down Frederick Street in the New Town of Edinburgh, with the castle in the old town just about visible in the distance. Spoiling the view is a misspelt sign warning of restricted access to "Princess" Street 80 yards ahead, which doesn't exist. It is meant to say Princes Street, which Frederick Street joins in a T-junction. While it's understandable error given the similarity in the words, it's still an odd one to make given that Princes Street is the main thoroughfare in the New Town, and is probably tied with the Royal Mile as the most famous streets in the capital. Presumably the source of the error is that whoever made the sign is not a local.

candidates.author: Dietmar Rabich
candidates.description: Colorful houses in Wale Street, Cape Town, Western Cape, South AfricaBo-Kaap is a historic neighborhood above the center of Cape Town. It was established in the 18th century when the Dutch colonial administration built houses for enslaved people from Southeast Asia, India, and East Africa. Many of them were Muslims and later became known as “Cape Malays”.After their liberation in the 19th century, Bo-Kaap developed into a center of Islamic culture in the Cape. Mosques such as the Auwal Mosque from 1794 bear witness to this tradition.The colourfully painted houses, originally an expression of newly won freedom, now characterise the image of the neighbourhood. Despite gentrification, Bo-Kaap remains an important symbol of cultural heritage and resilience in South Africa.
candidates.processing: EXIF orientation; RGB; maximum 1600px; JPEG quality 88; no generated edits
